hints: Start by picturing the order of a heartbeat - the top chambers squeeze first, then after a short pause the bottom chambers squeeze. What two jobs are needed to make that happen?
Think about who starts a wave of excitation on its own without nerves, and who passes that wave onward but holds it back briefly so blood has time to move down.
To get all 3 marks you need points about both regions - link the starter to atrial contraction and link the relay to the delay plus passing to the ventricles.
walkthrough:
The SAN Starts It All**
Your heart can beat by itself because a small patch of muscle in the wall of the right atrium fires off electrical signals regularly. This is the SAN. Because it sets the rate and rhythm on its own, we call it the pacemaker.

From SAN To Atrial Squeeze**
When the SAN fires, a wave of excitation spreads quickly across the walls of both atria. That wave makes the atrial muscle contract together. That is atrial systole, which pushes blood down into the ventricles.

The AVN Pauses Then Passes On**
The excitation cannot go straight into the ventricles because non-conducting tissue blocks it. Instead the AVN, found between the atria, picks it up and relays it onward to the bundle of His. Crucially it imposes a delay of about 0.1-0.2 s, giving time for the ventricles to fill completely before they contract.

Final answer: SAN acts as pacemaker, sending out waves of excitation / depolarisation that initiate atrial systole. AVN relays impulses to the bundle of His after a short delay to allow atria to empty / ventricles to fill before ventricular systole.

hints: Compare wall thickness to lumen size for high pressure versus low pressure flow, and remember which vessel is only one cell thick for exchange.
walkthrough:
Match Structure To Pressure**
Vessels with three layers split into two types. The one with a thick wall relative to lumen diameter withstands high pressure near the heart, so that is the artery (E). The one with a thin wall and wide lumen carries low pressure blood back, so that is the vein (D). A wall of only one layer can only be the tiny exchange vessel, the capillary (F).
Final answer: D = vein, E = artery, F = capillary.

hints: Picture the very innermost lining that touches blood - how many cells thick must it be to be smooth and not block flow?
Recall the name and shape given to flat, thin lining cells that make a smooth pavement-like surface.
walkthrough:
A Lining Built For Smooth Flow**
Endothelium lines all vessels. It is only one cell thick, so it does not narrow the lumen or obstruct blood.

Flat Pavement Cells**
The cells are squamous - very thin and flattened like paving stones fitted edge to edge. That gives a smooth surface facing the blood, reducing friction and preventing clotting and allowing easy diffusion in capillaries.
Final answer: Single layer / one cell thick; made of flattened / thin squamous (pavement) epithelial cells with a smooth surface facing the lumen.
